summary:
Hidalgo stands under Mexico's national framework, in which legal gender recognition is established state by state rather than by a single federal statute. No Hidalgo-specific enactment, administrative procedure or documented incident affecting trans people is supported by the sources assembled for this record.

As of March 2025, 22 of Mexico's 32 states had enacted an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, two more operate such a procedure in practice without having legislated it, six state legislatures have enacted nothing, and only seven states extend recognition to children. Human Rights Watch called on the states without procedures to adopt them and warned that implementation differs sharply from one state to another.

The Supreme Court of Mexico set binding guidelines for the states and extended the right to recognition to minors in 2022, and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights requires a simple, accessible procedure. Where no procedure exists, Human Rights Watch documents identity-document mismatch driving discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, with incidents of that kind recorded in Guanajuato and Tabasco.
tangentialFactors:
Violence against trans people intensified over the year to mid-2024. AP reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, and the killings drew LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months.

Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100.

One legislature has moved to close a specific gap. Mexico City's Congress approved the "Paola Buenrostro law" in July 2024, criminalising transfemicide; the statute takes its name from a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished.

The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that all LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.

Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice, and cautions that this must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.
localsOnly:
The Human Rights Watch and Community Center for Inclusion report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" (6 March 2024) documents what silence in a state statute means for residents on the ground. In Tabasco, without identity documents matching a trans person's gender, every document request or appearance scrutiny carries risk of violence, harassment and humiliation, and trans people are excluded from employment, health services, education and financial transactions. The report was set against the August 2023 murder of trans woman Karina Gomez in Villahermosa and against more than 95% of homicides nationally going unpunished in 2022.

Partnership recognition is settled at the national level: same-sex marriage has been legal across Mexico since 2009, with Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction.
outOfScopeNotes:
Hidalgo's own legislative position on legal gender recognition is not sourced here: whether the state has enacted an administrative procedure, whether one operates in practice, and whether Hidalgo extends recognition to minors are all unresolved on the available inventory.

Enforcement of the Supreme Court's binding guidelines within Hidalgo, and any documented case of document-request obstruction, discrimination or violence against a trans person in Hidalgo, are not addressed by the sources and remain unverified. The inventory also carries nothing on bathroom or facilities rules, health-care access, hate-crime protection or partner recognition as they apply inside Hidalgo specifically.
